paragraphs: Joseph Wolins Edited
This is going to be in color, I assume.
Yeah, it's going to be in color. I'll show you.
No, no, no.
I'll show you where it looks like.
Only because we have an antiquated TV set, black and white.

Okay. Okay. So, can you tell me about the first time you met Maurice Sievan? Yes, I believe it was at the Contemporary Arts Gallery, which was at that time on East 57th Street. It was a gallery open to obscure unknown artists. That goes way back after the WPA period, 1950, 50, 49 rather, 51. And we exhibited together at that particular gallery. It's no longer in existence, but it was a very popular, well-known, and highly esteemed gallery at the time.
Do you remember any anecdotes about Maurice from that gallery showing or the work that he was showing?

No particular recollection except that the woman who ran the gallery, Miss Emily Francis, was a rather somewhat of a tyrannical elderly woman who bullied and abused us whenever she can. But basically she was a very kind woman. I remember her yelling at Maurice for some infraction at the time and he, she accepted her criticism and I told him that was very good of him, very strategic and he behaved himself very well. That's about the only thing I recall in the gallery. He exhibited with us right along for a number of years. It was called the Contemporary Arts Gallery at that time. And I recall earlier of course when he was on a federal art project, the WPA with me, with us, but he moved in another area, another field, and I think he was a much more

explorative experimental artist than I was at the time. We were in our middle 20s of course, you realize that. And I did meet him in Rockport, Massachusetts. He and his wife came up there during the summer period to paint, like all of us. And we congregated together after dinner, usually. And there were so many of us at the time that I couldn't clearly single them out. Tell me about the vacation in Rockport.

It wasn't a vacation. It was a time for actually working. We took off our job. We fled from New York, and we had simple accommodations in this particular place above Boston, where it's located, Cape Ann. And we went there to work, to paint, to do our sculpture. And we got up early in the morning, and we didn't leave the entirely bohemian life that's commonly expected from Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer. and others, we were very, very much concerned about our development as creative people. And Maurice was one of them, like ourselves. Do you remember some of the pieces or some of the types of work that Maurice was doing up there?

Not entirely. I remember he was working on landscapes, I believe. The interior of Cape Ann, where Rockport was located, there was a quarry which is filled with natural springs and people bathed there, usually in the nude at night. We went there not to see these bathers but we went there to paint. And Maurice was there also painting. We never disturbed each other. We just came there to paint. That was one of the stimulating, exciting parts of the summers of 1942 to '47, I think it was right through for five years.
Really?
Yeah.
Okay, so can you tell me a little bit about, I know on the phone you told me that you got your WPA grant at the same time basically as Maurice did. Can you tell me about that? I really don't know.

Well, I want to clarify that. It wasn't a grant. Realistically, it was a welfare concern by the Roosevelt administration. It was the first time in the history of the United States, the wealthiest country in the world, that decided to do something for artists, musicians, architects, painters, sculptors, and so on. And this was a renaissance actually in a sense. It lasted from 1935 to

1942. And it wasn't a grant, as you say. It was an economic need. And what may surprise a great many people, and will take away the glamour of this period, is that we had to apply for welfare. You had to apply for welfare. You got about $7 a week for food, lodging, rent, and so on. this is what you lived on. After that first stage, if you were a professional within the arts, you applied for a position on the Federal Art Project, which was called the Works Projects Administration, or WPA. And we applied. Those of us who are lucky were accepted, and we worked on the WPA as teachers, art teachers, music teachers, architects. We did research in early American architecture. The fortunate ones in mural paintings, graphic works, easel paintings, sculpture, and so on. And it was one of the most remarkable periods in the cultural history of the United States. And it's about eight, no, about 10 years ago, John O'Connor, who writes for the New York Times, I think, re-evaluated, rediscovered this, and wrote a book in 1981. And that exploded the entire art world here in the United States. And a re-evaluation took place, and everybody became interested. To such an extent, there was a great demand for this work. There wasn't much left of it, but everybody began to buy things, the museums especially, and galleries began to reap profits from the selling of the WPA work. To such an extent that I began to handle my old WPA work with kid gloves. Where one time I used to throw them around. They suddenly became valuable. That's why I told these chaps to be careful when they put these things back. Fifteen years ago, I wouldn't care if they fell down. We couldn't give them away. Nobody wanted them. Now we're discovering, I discover that relatives who reluctantly accepted them as gifts were very glad to get rid of them. I didn't tell them why, but I was going to get fabulous prices for them, otherwise they wouldn't return them. So I got them all back and I had a series of exhibitions in Washington, New York, Sarasota and Florida recently, and Los Angeles. just WPA. But now that I'm older and I've left that particular period, I identify myself as living and working and eating in 1991, so that I'm more interested in having my current work exposed, seen, and hopefully acquired by collectors and museums. But that's a big battle. Are you recording all this?
Yeah.
Good Lord.

Now, can you tell me, how did Maurice fit in with the WPA artists. He was just one in a ditch. He was just one of six, seven hundred artists within New York City, or if not more. And he didn't, there was no, he just had to obey to some extent the requirements and the needs of the administration. Some of us rebelled and broke laws and painted pictures and sculpture which made the administration frown and become embarrassed, but they eventually treasured them, and they are now in museums.

And tell me about what kind of person was he? I mean, you spent time painting with him and everything. Give me a little bit about, you know, how did he act when he painted? How did he go out and paint?

How did he go out? He just put on the roughest clothes, the way those chaps are, so you can't use clean clothes. You put on your roughest clothes, you bid goodbye to your wife and kids if You had them at the age of 22 and you left and came back with a collection of work which was either accepted or frowned upon or purchased. And like all of us, there's nothing unique or unusual. Some artists at the time didn't go out and paint. They painted in their studios. It was just a question of temperament, personality, and needs at the time. So there's nothing particularly... I hope I'm not belittling Mr. Sievan but he just fit into a niche like all of us did. We couldn't afford to be, work was very important, you see. And we got up at 5, 6 o'clock in the morning and got our equipment geared together and started to work, sometimes for 5, 6, 7 hours standing up. That's why we all have fallen arches.
Can you tell me what kind of person he was?

Well, it's hard to say. Over the years, he was rather outgoing, cheerful. He smiled when the occasion called for it. And there's nothing singular or unusual. He didn't beat anybody up. He didn't steal anything. He behaved himself. We had to, you see, the artist has to, to the general public, it's very difficult to understand that we have to conserve ourselves. If we become erratically temperamental, you can't work. If we abuse our environment or our family or our children or the mailman, we can't function. So it's very important. It might seem to the average layperson a rather selfish and self-centered attitude, but in order to work, You just have to do this. Ask Picasso. He was a night person, of course. He worked right through the night and never got up until 12 o'clock. I can't afford to do that.

Right. Now, the more I'm learning about Maurice Sievan and talking with people and just seeing the size of the estate and what he left, he really didn't like to sell his work or part with it. Can you just talk about that a little?

I certainly can. That was, that's the most misanthropic and wrong attitude to take. And I've had the same attitude, but I've learned realistically, like all of us have to. You can't hoard your poetry in your dresser drawer. The world has to see it. And all cultures, the artwork was done for the church, for the state, for the religion, for patrons, for the public. And now we don't have those things. To replace patronage and private patronage, we have museums, which is a

different, which is something which evolved out of the 18th, 19th century. But we cannot, it was wrong of him to take that attitude. Whatever psychological or disturbance there was, or whatever fear there was, usually, or whatever insecurity there was, and I know artists who are like that, it's difficult to face the reality and exposure of a critical world. So what you do, you withdraw. And I'm afraid Maurice did.
Yeah, it's interesting because at the time, when he was showing his work, he was getting critical acclaim. People generally liked his work.

Well, liking it is one aspect of it, of course. All the great artists of the past had to fight their way for exposure and for recognition. It's inexcusable. It has to be done. It's a difficult road to follow, but if you read the lives of all artists, they all had to fight their way. It's not easy. No one likes it. I certainly don't. And I'm right in the thick of it. At my age, I should retire and be happy and content and sit in a rocking chair. But I can't afford to. I find that attitude in this particular painter very, very bad. I know others like it today.

Now, on that particular subject, we're not going to hear my question. So if we could rephrase that a little bit so that you could put the question into your answer so that we know what you're talking about. Let me ask you again. Why was it that Maurice didn't like to sell his work or part with his work?

Well, simply it was a wrong and fearful insecurity because it's unreal. A doctor doesn't do that. An architect doesn't do it. A sonographer doesn't do that. He says, why should an artist do that? someone I know my former wife to be exact is reluctant to sell her work and I ask her why she says oh she loves everything she does I said well after 10 years you won't be able to move in your house in your studio there's such a vast collection what will you do the same with Maurice

can you give me a little experience first hand experience or anecdote about Maurice holding on to his work and not wanting to show it? Do you remember any instances when that happened? Well, I vaguely recall over a long time ago, we had an exhibition here in New York, and I think he took his work back after the exhibition, if I'm not mistaken. He didn't want nobody to buy it. And Miss Frances, who ran the gallery, was appalled by this rather childish or hoarding of one's treasures. I'm very much opposed to it because I know people have suffered unnecessarily, unconsciously, when they really do this.

Yeah, can we kind of go back and talk about this one particular instance? And if you can use Maurice's name a little bit in your answer, That way we'll know. Well, I can understand the importance of this, but I can say that Maurice Sievan had the largest collection of Maurice Sievan's in the world. Does that cover it? And can you say that and tell me why?

For the simple reason that he's reluctant to give them up. They're treasures in the eyes. Or are they? I don't know. You see, I don't know. I know so many people like this. They eventually learn like I have had to myself. You see, I have the largest collection of my own. And I need space. I need work space, as you can recognize. And I want to get rid of them. I need the floor. And your equipment may be here for the next five years. And how will I be able to paint with all this on the floor? So I got to, it's a reality. Michelangelo did not take his frescoes in the Sistine Chapel after they were finished. They were exposed to the world. So Maurice Sievan should have left his work exposed to the world as well. I think we covered that thoroughly, don't you? That's great. Now, let me just ask you, to follow up on that, if Maurice Sievan had shown his work more, if more museums had had it, if they were all in private collections over the years, do you think that he would hold a different spot in the history of art? To some extent.
Can you put my question into that?

Well, when an artist recognizes and sees his work in public view in museums and collections, There's a feeling of gratification. There's a further value that he recognizes that his work moves ahead out of his own life, out of his workshop, out of his studio. And now he's exposed practically naked to the whole world. And that's very valuable. And being exposed that way, you're subject to both kinds of criticism, complimentary, negative, whatever. But that's very essential for growth, to be out in the open.
Did Maurice ever talk to you about Kierkegaard or metaphysics?

No. He didn't. Maybe he recognized that it was a field that I couldn't enter it, or he may have made an attempt to and I just ignored it perhaps, or we were looking at some girls down at the beach and I couldn't concentrate on philosophical thought. That may have happened. So that was part of his personality which I knew nothing about.
What kind of things did you talk about?

Sex, food, and culture. That's an exhausting subject. Three, don't you think? Three of them together. And when you mix them together, you're exhausted at the end of the day. Now, can you expand on that a little bit? Because we're actually, it's very interesting. We're looking at his works now. We have almost his complete collection. And we're trying to get a little insight into how he thought about things, the kind of things that he was thinking of at the time.

Well, you can't read a person's thoughts and tendencies if they don't reveal much themselves. Maurice Sievan was not an extroverted, as I remember. He wasn't a loquacious or talkative person. He just – he had the typical characteristic of our male society. Do you know what I'm referring to?
Can you tell me?

Yeah. It's the macho personality which is cultivated here. You keep your mouth shut. You don't say much. You don't reveal your emotions. And if there's a death in the family, you don't cry. This is a male macho temperament. And Maurice was like that. I hope some of that will eventually change. Men are supposed to show their feelings, like children, like women, like people, generally. But we don't, do we?
Do you think that he saved those feelings for his work?

It could be, but his work didn't have the... It was not, as far as I recall, it wasn't a very intensely emotional kind of work, which was characteristic at the time of a certain school of painters called expressionists. They were a volatile, demanding, explosive direction, and Maurice was not of that school. I hope I'm not negating any of these things.

No, no, not at all. I mean, all this is great. No, no, there's... I have a film clip of Maurice painting, and it seems like he would paint out of the back of his car. He would have his whole painting set up in his trunk, and he would just drive somewhere and pull up and open up his trunk, and paint. Did you ever witness any of that or did you see him?

No, for the simple reason that he kept much of this, much of this kind of approach in his work to himself. He didn't, if I'd see him, it was no issue. It was no, we all did things like that, more or less.
We all did things like what? We're not hearing my question.

Oh, well, we all worked under the circumstances, and out of a car, inside the car while we were having lunch, we could be necking in the car with one hand and painting with the other. You follow me? It's simply that the circumstances were such that you accommodated yourself to the situation. If Maurice had to work out of his car, it was just he was getting his equipment out of there, which he carried, and it was easy for him to work directly. Nothing unusual, but. Now, in this home clip also, there's a crowd of people around him. He must be out in Central Park. Danny, we gotta change the tape.
Yeah.
Stop the beta cam. And Charles Hawthorne, were you at the Royal Academy of Design? Were you there at the same time as Maurice?
Well, I was there from 1931 to 1934. I don't know. He may have been there that particular period.

Tell me what it was like to study under Leon Kroll. Was Charles Hawthorne also? No, he died in 1928, 1929. Charles Hawthorne did. So I didn't know him at the time. Well, tell me what it was like to study under Leon Kroll. What kind of techniques did he, you know?

Leon Kroll was the best instructor at the National Academy of Design. He introduced the students to a whole vast background of painting specifically. And unlike the other instructors who were quite dreary and dull, Leon Kroll was the most forceful personality. He worked within a strict traditional manner himself and encouraged that, of course, so that we worked within that academic or conservative tradition. All of us did. God help us if we didn't, we'd be kicked out. But it was well known, it was one of the most famous and oldest art school within that conservative direction. And Leon Kroll was a very, very, very all-around alive person. And he lived up in Rockport, by coincidence, where I was staying. But I never met him up there. I was merely a student in New York City. And so was Maurice Sievan But I think Maurice was there slightly earlier than I was.
I think he was there in the early 20s.
Was he then?
Yeah. I have it written down at home.
Yeah, see, I don't...

But knowing the way Leon Kroll taught, this is very interesting because obviously you both came out of the same... Teaching background. Teaching background, so there's a lot of similarities there. What do you think, knowing Maurice and his work, what do you think Leon Kroll gave to Maurice?

Well, not only to Maurice, but to all of us. He gave us... (Phone rings) Can I get that? Yeah, why don't we stop, too? Are we rollin'? Okay. So, again, I think we got interrupted in there. And if you could put the question back into it specifically as it relates to Maurice, what do you think Leon Kroll gave to Maurice?

Well, as I said, he gave the very same thing he gave to all of us. You can't single out what he gave to Maurice alone because it was a large class. And there were three sessions in the school where Leon Kroll taught, one morning, one afternoon, two afternoons. And what he gave us was an appreciation and a recognition of certain Italian painters. I very clearly remember this. Whether these painters are known to the general public or not. But one thing I do recall, Leon

Kroll opened up a recognition of the early 15th century Italian Renaissance to us. And particularly a painter by the name of Piero della Francesca. That was a big, important thing in all of our in this class. And my interest in that particular Italian painter continues up to the present time. And I think it did for the other art students. It even affected all work. It was the kind of influence that affected well-known artists in their early period. For example, the early work of Arshile Gorky, William de Kooning, and William Baziotes. These are well-known artists with high reputations. Their early work showed the influence of the early Italians, as well as Picasso, of course. but this influence affected all of us and we to a great extent myself so that was what he gave us which I appreciate very much today so when I'm going back to Italy in a couple of months I'm going to a particular place to see the frescoes of Piero della Francesca I got that from Leon Kroll

now what is it about the art of that period that Leon Kroll was trying to impress so much on A kind of a certain stark simplicity and a very strong singular detachment, which is a characteristic of early Renaissance. And Piero della Francesca epitomizes that particular point of view. Wow.
Okay.
I'm giving you an art education.
Yeah.
I'm giving you a background.
I appreciate it tremendously.
Do you really?
Is there anything else that you can tell me about Maurice Sievan? Anything at all? I've covered almost everything except his eating habits. What more can I give you?

His eating habits. Well, no, I've asked you a lot of questions, and there might be things now that you might remember that I'm not covering. You knew him. I never knew him. Is there anything that you can tell me about Maurice Sievan?

Good Lord, I know. He put on his clothes in the morning like everybody else did. He ate a dreadful breakfast like we all did and got ulcers afterwards. And what else? He just lived the life of a typical New Yorker. He lived in New York, didn't he? I thought he lived out in a great somewhere, a suburb. But anyway.
Jackson Heights.
Jackson Heights. God, that's awful. But anyway, and he just survived more or less the way we all did with our problems and nothing singular or unique about this extraordinary American. painter.
Last question. Why is it that Maurice Sievan never made an impact in American art? That's a loaded question.
I'm gonna ask it anyway.

I could tell you in all frankness, but will this be publicized? Well, this will be I don't know that I'll even use your answer. We have a lot of pieces from you, but I'm just very interested because it seems that some artists make it. I mean, he was best friends with Mark Rothko and, you know, see where he is. I don't know. Why do some artists make an impact in art while others don't?

Well, there are certain specific reasons why that happens. In certain classical examples, artists could be very great, very fine, and totally neglected their entire life. The classical example is Vincent van Gogh, who never had a show in his entire life. I don't think he ever sold a single painting. But that's something else. The politics of art today is such that you have to be groomed by outside forces, by museums, art galleries, and patronage. It doesn't matter whether you're good or bad. You could be one of the worst artists, but if you have good publicity and the manipulative personality and know just what to do, you'll get in. And the other

extreme from Vincent Van Gogh, I can put my neck out and be killed if this is going to be exposed, is Andy Warhol, who in my estimation is an embarrassment. But he's highly recognized. His work is sought after. People fight over his work and so on. But time is a cruel thing, and that will show really later on what will happen. So that you, in Maurice's case, I believe that the combination of his recessiveness and withdrawal from the art scene, the fact that there's nothing unique or startling or original in his work, It's very eclectic, absorbed from other sources, including Mark Rothko and others. These are the facts. It doesn't have to be an artist's opinion. You say honest or artist? We're recording. Okay, we're rolling?
Okay.
This is the absolute last question. I'm sorry we ran out of tape before. Again, why is it that some artists make it and some artists don't?
Now do I have to remember what I said? No, not exactly.
Specifically with the case of Maurice Sievan.

Well, in the case of Maurice Sievan, his reluctance to expose himself in the world, which is absolutely essential, his reluctance to sell his work, was a bad point in his career. It's a bad point in anybody's career. You have to recognize these and you have to come out and show your work. If you don't, you're left in obscurity. And the art world is a very ruthless, realistic and harsh world where you're just brushed aside. Thousands of very fine accomplished artists has had this tragic thing happen to them by either indifference or fear, whatever it is. And in his case, the reason he didn't become recognized to any great extent is his own personality. He may be a very great artist, but that doesn't enter into it in our realistic world. It's quite different than what I said.
No, that's good. That's excellent. Now, I'll ask you again. Is there anything else that you can tell me about Maurice Sievan? Just anything at all.
I think we've covered this extraordinary person, haven't we, in every area?
When was the last time you saw him?

Oh, ten years ago, perhaps. I don't know, eight, ten years ago. Or it may have been earlier at an art exhibition or a museum. We just greet each other, as we usually do. And I think his wife was here.
Was that at the Queens Museum?

No, no. I think it was the Brooklyn Museum or the Museum of Modern Art. I don't remember. You couldn't recall for me just briefly the very last time you saw him? Well, you see, I couldn't because he was not a very close friend of mine. And over the years, I'd meet many former friends or friends who I'm still involved with constantly. We meet each other at galleries, museums, funerals, picnics, everywhere. So it's very difficult for me to recall the last time I saw him truthfully. When we move away from that, and he lived out further away, I rarely see him coming into Manhattan. Jackson Heights is quite a distance away from the art world, unfortunately. Is my voice clear enough? I don't know. Yeah. Very last question, and I promise this is really the last one. If you could write an epitaph. Will that be recorded?
Yes, that's recorded. This is the last question.
The last question.

If you could write an epitaph for Maurice Sievan, what would you say? Well, forgive the association, but the epitaph for Franz Schubert, was something to the effect that if he had lived longer, there had been much more of his great paintings. In Schubert's case, more of his great music. What was his age when he died? I don't even remember. 83.

Oh, well that's hardly a fair question. A fair answer to your question. However, I couldn't know it. I don't even know where he's buried. I don't even know what could one... I'm sure the tombstone indicates his birth, his day he left this earth. And what more can you write? Have you ever been to Paris to Pere-Lachaise?
- No.

- Go there, it's a fascinating place. Everybody goes there, it's like a picnic ground. It's the most fascinating place in all of Paris. Few Americans go there, but when they discovered it's a place to spend hours. On each tombstone, there's an expression about the artist or scientist in a great, great place.
Okay.
God, that's an awful thing to finish...
No. No. Okay. We're done. Cut tape Danny. Okay. Well, thank you.
